title: The Tiger King
summary: Kalki's satire tells of a Maharaja who, warned that a tiger will cause his death, sets out to kill a hundred tigers to defeat the prophecy. The story mocks the vanity and whims of those in power and shows, through dramatic irony, that fate and nature cannot be bullied.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Kalki (R. Krishnamurthy, 1899–1954) was a celebrated Tamil writer, journalist and freedom fighter. This story, translated from Tamil, is a political satire on the princely rulers of colonial India.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram is told at birth that he will be killed by a tiger. He kills ninety-nine tigers and believes he has shot the hundredth, but his bullet misses. He finally dies from an infection caused by a splinter from a cheap wooden toy tiger. The 'hundredth tiger' takes its revenge.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
• The prophecy: Astrologers predict that the royal baby will one day meet his death. The ten-day-old infant astonishes everyone by speaking and asking the manner of his death. The chief astrologer says that, being born in the hour of the Bull, he must fear the tiger.
  • The vow: When he comes to power at twenty, he kills his first tiger. The astrologer warns that he may kill ninety-nine but must beware the hundredth. The king bans tiger hunting by anyone else in the state.
  • Risk to the throne: A high-ranking British officer wants to hunt tigers there. The king refuses even a photograph with a dead tiger. To save his kingdom he sends some fifty diamond rings to the officer's wife, expecting her to choose one or two; she keeps them all. The bill is about three lakh rupees.
  • Marriage for tigers: After seventy kills the tigers in his state are extinct, so he marries a princess from a state with a large tiger population and reaches ninety-nine.
  • The hundredth tiger: No tiger can be found. The king grows furious, raises taxes and dismisses officers. The frightened dewan secretly brings an old tiger from the People's Park in Madras and leaves it in the forest. The king fires; the weak tiger faints from shock but is not hit. Afraid of losing their jobs, the hunters kill it themselves and say nothing.
  • The end: On his son's third birthday the king buys a crude wooden tiger. A tiny sliver pierces his right hand; the wound becomes infected, surgeons operate, and the king dies.

notes.heading: Themes and satire
notes.html:
• Arrogance of power: the king uses the state's resources, his marriage and his officials only to serve a personal obsession.
  • Satire on rulers and their servility to the British: he protects his throne through an expensive bribe.
  • Satire on sycophants: ministers and hunters lie out of fear.
  • Cruelty to animals and ecological imbalance: a whole population of tigers is wiped out for one man's ego.
  • Fate: human effort cannot overturn destiny; pride invites a fall.

notes.heading: Character sketch and dramatic irony
notes.html:
The Maharaja: brave and determined, but vain, stubborn, whimsical and self-centred. He neglects his people, punishes on impulse and places his own safety above everything. His courage is real, yet it serves only his ego.

The dewan: clever and practical, but a flatterer who acts to save his position.

Dramatic irony: the reader knows the hundredth tiger survived the king's shot, while the king celebrates his victory over fate. The final irony is that a lifeless toy, bought for a trifling sum, does what a hundred real tigers could not.

notes.heading: Title and message
notes.html: The title is apt and ironic: he is 'Tiger King' because he killed tigers, and also because a tiger brought his end. The story warns against misuse of power, blind pride and the thoughtless killing of wildlife.

questions.q: Why was the Maharaja called the Tiger King?
questions.answerHtml: It was foretold that a tiger would cause his death. To disprove this he made tiger hunting the mission of his life and killed ninety-nine tigers. His obsession with tigers, and his eventual death because of one, earned him the name.

questions.q: How did the dewan arrange the hundredth tiger?
questions.answerHtml: Fearing the king's rage, the dewan had an old tiger brought from the People's Park in Madras. He and his wife dragged it to the forest at night in a car and left it where the king was hunting.

questions.q: How did the hundredth tiger take its revenge?
questions.answerHtml: The real hundredth tiger escaped the king's bullet. Later a splinter from a wooden toy tiger pierced the king's hand; the infection spread and he died after an operation. Thus a tiger, though only a toy, fulfilled the prophecy.

questions.q: The story is a satire on the conceit of those in power. Comment.
questions.answerHtml:
Kalki exposes how absolute power breeds self-importance. The Maharaja treats the kingdom as his private property. He bans others from hunting tigers, threatens to confiscate the wealth of anyone who harms one, raises taxes when he is frustrated and dismisses officers on a whim.

His priorities are absurd. To protect a personal vow he risks his throne, then spends about three lakh rupees of public money on rings to please a British officer's wife. He even selects a bride according to the tiger population of her father's state. The people's welfare never enters his mind.

Those around him are no better: the dewan and the hunters flatter and deceive because they fear him. The ending completes the satire. A man who believed he had conquered destiny is brought down by a cheap toy. The writer shows that arrogance makes the powerful ridiculous, and that neither position nor force can defeat fate.

questions.q: What is the author's indirect comment on subjecting innocent animals to the wilfulness of human beings?
questions.answerHtml:
The story treats the killing of tigers in a mock-heroic tone, but the criticism is clear. A hundred animals are to die only because one man fears a prediction. The tigers have done no harm; they are victims of a ruler's ego.

The consequences are serious. Tigers become extinct in Pratibandapuram, and the king moves on to empty the forests of another state. This is the destruction of wildlife for vanity, not need. The old tiger from the park, too feeble to resist, is finally shot by hunters merely to save their jobs.

By letting the king die through a wooden tiger, the author suggests a kind of natural justice: those who are cruel to nature do not escape. The story therefore carries a conservation message. Human beings have no right to wipe out other creatures for sport or pride, and such wilfulness upsets the balance of nature.
